title: THE DEMONS OBEYED THEM… BUT JESUS SAID THEY WERE CELEBRATING THE WRONG THING.
paragraphs: THE DEMONS OBEYED THEM… BUT JESUS SAID THEY WERE CELEBRATING THE WRONG THING.

Seventy-two disciples returned with astonishing stories of spiritual victory. But one sentence from Jesus exposed a danger far more personal than demons: You can become so fascinated with what God does through you that you forget the greater miracle of what He has done for you.
“Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.” — Luke 10:20 (KJV)
Imagine standing in front of Jesus with the greatest testimony of your life.
Your hands are trembling. Your heart is racing. You have just witnessed things you never thought possible.
People who were oppressed have been set free. Darkness has retreated. Demons have submitted to the authority of Jesus' name.
And you cannot wait to tell Him.
“Lord, even the devils are subject unto us through thy name!” (Luke 10:17, KJV).
You expect Him to celebrate with you.
And in a sense, He does. He acknowledges the reality of Satan's defeat. He affirms the authority He has given His messengers.
But then He says something that must have stopped them in their tracks.
Do not make that your greatest reason to rejoice.
Rejoice because your names are written in heaven.
Wait.
They had just returned from confronting demonic powers.
They had witnessed the authority of Jesus overpower the forces of darkness.
They were celebrating something genuinely extraordinary.
So why would Jesus redirect their joy?
Because He knew something about the human heart that we are still struggling to understand two thousand years later.
It is possible to become so excited about being used by God that you slowly lose sight of the greater wonder of belonging to God.
And if that sentence makes you uncomfortable, stay with me.
Because this story is not merely about demons.
It is about the frightening possibility of measuring your spiritual life by what happens around you while neglecting what is happening within you.
It is about the difference between spiritual authority and spiritual security.
Between ministry success and salvation.
Between the applause of people and the grace of God.
And perhaps most personally, it is about the question we rarely ask ourselves when everything seems to be going well:
If God took away everything that makes me feel spiritually important, would Jesus Himself still be enough?
Before we answer, we need to return to the road where this extraordinary story began.
Jesus had appointed and sent out His disciples ahead of Him into the places He intended to visit.
Luke 10:1 records the number as seventy in some ancient manuscripts and seventy-two in others. This textual variation does not change the message of the passage.
They were not sent to build personal reputations.
They were not commissioned to become religious celebrities.
They were sent as messengers preparing the way for Jesus.

He told them that the harvest was plentiful but the laborers were few. He instructed them to pray for workers, to travel in dependence upon God, to proclaim that the kingdom of God had come near, and to minister in His name.
He also warned them that they were being sent like lambs among wolves.
Think about that.
Jesus did not promise them an easy assignment.
He sent them into a world where rejection was possible, hostility was real, and spiritual opposition was serious.
Yet when they returned, their hearts were overflowing.
Luke records their excitement:
“And the seventy returned again with joy, saying, Lord, even the devils are subject unto us through thy name.” (Luke 10:17, KJV)
Notice those final words.
“Through thy name.”
At this moment, they understood something essential.
The authority was not originally theirs.
It belonged to Jesus.
They were astonished that His name carried such power even when He was not physically standing beside them.
And Jesus did not tell them that their experience was imaginary.
He responded:
“I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.” (Luke 10:18, KJV)
This is one of the most striking statements in the passage.
The Greek reads:
Ἐθεώρουν τὸν Σατανᾶν ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεσόντα.
A close translation is:
“I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.”

The verb etheōroun (ἐθεώρουν) is an imperfect form of a verb meaning to watch or observe. The wording presents Jesus as witnessing Satan's fall, while the surrounding context connects His statement with the disciples' mission and the defeat of demonic opposition.

Christians have understood this saying in different ways. Some connect it with Satan's original downfall. Others understand it as a vision of Satan's authority being overthrown through the advance of Jesus' kingdom. Still others see the present victories as anticipating Satan's ultimate defeat.
The immediate context strongly emphasizes the defeat of Satan's power as the kingdom advances through Jesus.
But we should not force the verse to answer every question about Satan's history.
What is unmistakable is this:
The disciples were celebrating what had happened through their ministry.
Jesus was showing them that their experiences were part of something far greater than themselves.
The kingdom of God was breaking into a fallen world.
Satan's power was being challenged by the authority of the Son of God.
And yet, even with all of that happening, Jesus wanted their deepest joy anchored somewhere else.
He continued:
“Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy: and nothing shall by any means hurt you.” (Luke 10:19, KJV)
In this context, serpents and scorpions communicate the danger of hostile spiritual opposition, though Christians differ over whether the imagery also includes literal dangers.
The promise should not be twisted into permission to test God, deliberately handle dangerous animals, or assume that faithful Christians can never experience injury, persecution, or death.
Jesus Himself had already warned His followers that discipleship could involve suffering.
The point is that the authority of the enemy cannot overthrow the saving purpose and ultimate victory of Christ.
And then comes the sentence that changes everything.
“Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.” (Luke 10:20, KJV)
In the original Greek:
πλὴν ἐν τούτῳ μὴ χαίρετε ὅτι τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῖν ὑποτάσσεται, χαίρετε δὲ ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγγέγραπται ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς.
A close translation is:
“Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names have been written in heaven.”
There is a beautiful detail hidden in the Greek that deserves our attention.
The word translated “have been written” is engegraptai (ἐγγέγραπται), a perfect passive verb from engraphō, meaning to inscribe or register.
The perfect tense presents the names as having been written, with the resulting state continuing.
The passive voice emphasizes that the disciples are not the ones writing their own names into heaven's register.
This is not a picture of people earning their way into God's acceptance by collecting enough spiritual accomplishments.
It is a picture of a heavenly registration that gives them a reason for joy far deeper than their extraordinary ministry experiences.
The verse does not explain every detail of the doctrine of salvation, but its emphasis is unmistakable.
Their greatest treasure was not the authority they exercised over demons. It was their place among those who belong to God.
And here is where the story begins to reach into our lives.
Because most of us have never returned from a missionary journey reporting that demons submitted to us.
But we know what it feels like to find our identity in what we accomplish.
The pastor who feels valuable when the congregation is growing.
The worship leader who feels close to God when the room is emotionally moved.
The Christian content creator who feels spiritually successful when a post reaches thousands of people.
The ministry volunteer who secretly wonders whether anyone notices the sacrifices being made.
The believer who feels confident when prayers are answered quickly, but begins questioning God's love when heaven seems silent.
And perhaps the person reading this right now who has been serving everyone else while quietly falling apart inside.
You keep showing up.
You keep encouraging people.
You keep posting Scripture.
You keep telling others that God is faithful.
But when the phone is finally silent, the doors are closed, and nobody needs anything from you, an uncomfortable question begins whispering through your soul.
Does God still delight in me when I have nothing impressive to show Him?
Listen carefully.
Your worth before God is not established by your ministry statistics.
It is not measured by how many people know your name.
It is not proven by how dramatic your testimony sounds.
And it is not determined by whether you have experienced extraordinary spiritual manifestations.
Your deepest reason for rejoicing is Jesus Christ and the salvation He gives by grace.
That is what makes Luke 10:20 so powerful.
Jesus was not condemning the disciples for being happy about the defeat of evil.
He was correcting the foundation of their joy.
There is a difference.
He was not saying that deliverance was meaningless.
He was teaching that even the most remarkable spiritual victory must never become more precious to us than our relationship with God.
Because gifts can become idols.
Ministry can become identity.
Influence can become an addiction.
And even genuine experiences of God's power can become occasions for pride when our hearts begin focusing on ourselves.
This is why another teaching of Jesus should make us examine our lives with extraordinary seriousness.

In Matthew 7:22–23, Jesus warns that some people will appeal to their religious works, even claiming to have prophesied and cast out demons in His name, only to hear Him declare that He never knew them.
That passage is not teaching that every believer who experiences spiritual power is secretly lost.
Nor does it give us permission to judge another person's salvation based on the visibility of their ministry.
Its warning is more searching than that.
Religious accomplishments, even extraordinary claims of spiritual activity, are not a substitute for truly knowing Christ and doing the Father's will.
A person may know the language of ministry without possessing a heart surrendered to Jesus.
A person may impress a crowd while hiding an unrepentant life.
A person may become familiar with the things of God while remaining distant from God Himself.
And that should move us toward humility, not toward suspicion of everyone around us.
The first heart we must examine is our own.
Not with hopeless terror.
But with reverent honesty.
Because the same Jesus who warns us against false confidence also invites sinners to come to Him for mercy.
And perhaps this is the moment where the story becomes painfully personal.
What if you have been using your service to God as a way of avoiding surrender to God?
What if staying busy in ministry has become easier than confessing the sin you keep hiding?
What if you have become more concerned about protecting your Christian reputation than allowing Jesus to confront what is happening in your private life?
You can know the right verses and still need repentance.
You can speak about forgiveness and still struggle to forgive.
You can encourage people to pray while neglecting your own secret time with God.
You can tell everyone else that Jesus heals broken hearts while refusing to bring Him your own wounds.
And none of those struggles should drive you to despair.
They should drive you to Christ.
Because the answer to spiritual hypocrisy is not to become better at appearing holy.
It is to stop hiding and come honestly before the Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our religious image.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins through His death and to rise again in victory.
And that brings us to something even more astonishing than the disciples' authority over demons.
Think about the contrast.
The disciples were amazed that evil spirits submitted to them.
But the Gospel announces that the sinless Son of God willingly humbled Himself for sinners.
The One who possessed all authority became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:5–8).
The One before whom demons trembled allowed Himself to be mocked, beaten, and crucified.
Not because He was powerless.
But because He was accomplishing redemption.
Colossians 2:13–15 describes God's work in Christ as forgiving our trespasses, canceling the record of debt against us, and triumphing over the hostile powers through the cross.
The cross was not a defeat that Jesus barely survived.
It was central to God's victorious plan of salvation.
And the resurrection declared that death would not have the final word.
So when Jesus told His disciples to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, He was directing them toward a greater joy than their momentary experience of power.
The joy of belonging to the God who saves.
The joy of grace.
The joy of redemption.
The joy that does not depend upon whether today's ministry was impressive.
And that joy becomes especially precious when life stops looking victorious.
Because what happens when the crowd disappears?
What happens when the ministry struggles?
What happens when your prayers seem unanswered?
What happens when you are sick, exhausted, grieving, or too weak to serve the way you once did?
What happens when you are no longer the person everyone calls for encouragement, but the person who desperately needs someone to sit beside you and pray?
If your joy rests entirely upon what God is doing through you, suffering can make you feel spiritually worthless.
But if your joy rests in Christ and His saving grace, suffering cannot erase the Gospel.
Your circumstances may change.
Your strength may fail.
Your influence may diminish.
Your abilities may be limited.
But the finished work of Jesus does not become less sufficient when your life becomes difficult.
This does not mean believers never experience doubt, sorrow, or spiritual dryness.
It means that the ground of our hope is greater than our changing emotions.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this today.
You are not less loved because you are tired.
You are not more saved because you are successful.
You do not become more worthy of God's grace because people admire your spiritual gifts.
And you cannot purchase His acceptance with years of religious service.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together beautifully.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
Good works are the fruit of God's saving grace, not the price we pay to obtain it.
We do not serve Jesus to convince Him to become our Savior.
We serve because He is our Savior.
And when that truth settles deeply into your heart, something changes.
You can serve without needing applause.
You can give without needing recognition.
You can rejoice when another person's ministry grows.
You can confess weakness without feeling that your entire identity is collapsing.
You can repent when the Holy Spirit exposes sin instead of desperately defending your image.
Because your hope is no longer built upon the illusion that you are extraordinary.
Your hope is built upon the extraordinary mercy of Jesus Christ.
There is another beautiful detail in Luke 10 that many readers pass over too quickly.
Immediately after Jesus redirects the disciples' joy, Luke tells us that Jesus Himself rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and praised the Father (Luke 10:21).
The passage does not end with Jesus crushing their enthusiasm.
It moves into the joy of Jesus Himself.
He praises the Father for revealing divine truth to those who receive it with childlike dependence rather than self-sufficient pride.
What a contrast.
The disciples are excited about authority.
Jesus rejoices in the Father's gracious revelation.
The disciples are astonished by what they have accomplished.
Jesus directs attention to what God has graciously given.
And then He privately tells His disciples that their eyes are blessed to see what prophets and kings had longed to see (Luke 10:23–24).
Their greatest privilege was not simply that demons submitted.
It was that they were witnessing the fulfillment of God's saving purposes in Jesus Christ.
They were standing in the presence of the promised Messiah.
And that is the heart of this entire story.
The greatest gift of Christianity is not that Jesus gives us access to extraordinary experiences. The greatest gift is that through Jesus, sinners can be reconciled to God.
Think about how that changes the way we pray.
Instead of only asking, “Lord, use me powerfully,” we begin praying, “Lord, make me faithful.”
Instead of only asking, “Lord, increase my influence,” we begin praying, “Lord, increase my love for You.”
Instead of only asking, “Lord, let people see what You can do through me,” we begin praying, “Lord, let people see Jesus in the way I live.”
And instead of measuring every day by visible victories, we learn to treasure the quiet work of grace.
The apology nobody saw.
The temptation resisted in secret.
The bitter heart finally choosing forgiveness.
The weary believer opening Scripture again.
The broken person whispering, “Lord, have mercy on me.”
The Christian who has fallen into sin, stops making excuses, and comes to Jesus in genuine repentance.
These moments may never become viral testimonies.
But they matter.
Not because they earn salvation, but because God's grace transforms real lives.
And if you are reading this while carrying the weight of a spiritual failure, please do not misunderstand the message.
Jesus is not inviting you to become obsessed with whether you have done enough to deserve heaven.
You have not.
Neither have I.
That is why grace is grace.
Romans 3:23–24 teaches that all have sinned and that justification is given freely by God's grace through the redemption found in Christ Jesus.
The answer to our sin is not self-congratulation.
It is repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you have been living a double life, do not use grace as an excuse to continue hiding.
Bring your sin into the light.
Turn away from what is destroying your fellowship with God and harming others.
Seek forgiveness.
Make things right where you can.
Receive the mercy that Christ offers.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive confessed sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not permission to love darkness.
It is an invitation to stop running from the Light.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe it is private.
Maybe people know what happened.
Maybe nobody knows except God.
Maybe you have been judged by others.
Maybe the harshest voice you hear is your own.
But the Gospel does not begin with the announcement that you are beyond redemption.
It begins with the good news of what God has done in Jesus Christ.
And the same Savior who called sinners to repentance still calls people to Himself.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not merely a slogan.
Not because Jesus pretends our sins never happened.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because consequences always disappear.
But because Christ can forgive the guilty, restore the repentant, and transform lives that seemed beyond hope.
He does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
He rewrites the future of those who come to Him by grace.
And perhaps the most unforgettable part of Luke 10:20 is that Jesus tells His disciples to rejoice in something they cannot see with their physical eyes.
They could see the results of their ministry.
They could hear the testimonies.
They could witness the submission of evil spirits.
But they could not look into heaven and inspect the divine register.
They had to trust the word of Jesus.
And so do we.
The Christian's assurance must rest upon the promises of God in Christ, not upon extraordinary experiences or human achievements.
Jesus says in John 6:37 that the one who comes to Him He will never cast out.
And in John 10:27–29, He speaks of His sheep hearing His voice, following Him, receiving eternal life, and being held securely in His hand and the Father's hand.
These promises call us to faith in Christ, not confidence in ourselves.
There is a related image in Revelation 20:12–15, where the book of life appears in the solemn scene of final judgment.
And Revelation 21:27 speaks of those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life.
The imagery is deeply serious.
Eternal life is not a minor benefit attached to Christianity.
It is a gift of immeasurable worth, received through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
That is why the question Jesus raises is so much greater than whether we have ever witnessed a miracle.
The question is whether we truly belong to Him.
Not whether we can impress Him.
Not whether we can perform for Him.
Not whether we can build a reputation in His name.
But whether we have come to Him in repentance and faith.
And if that question has exposed something in your heart today, do not rush past it.
Put down the performance.
Stop pretending you are spiritually stronger than you are.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive testimony before coming to Jesus.
You need the Savior.
Perhaps your prayer today is as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have loved recognition more than obedience. Forgive me for measuring my worth by what I accomplish instead of resting in Your grace. Expose the pride I have excused, the sins I have hidden, and the fears I have allowed to control me. Teach me to rejoice in You above every gift, every achievement, and every spiritual experience. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I turn to You for mercy. Make my life a testimony of Your grace, not my greatness. Amen.”
If that prayer reflects what is happening in your heart, you do not have to pretend that everything is already fixed.
Repentance is not a performance.
Healing and growth often take time.
And discipleship is not a single emotional moment followed by a life without struggle.
It is a continuing walk of faith, obedience, dependence, and grace.
You do not need to share details you are not ready to make public. A simple, sincere response is enough.
And if you have experienced God's forgiveness and restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading silently may need to be reminded that repentance is possible and grace is real.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message more than you realize.
Perhaps it is a pastor carrying the invisible weight of ministry.
Perhaps it is a believer whose faith has become tangled with the pressure to succeed.
Perhaps it is someone who has stopped attending church because they believe their failures have disqualified them from ever coming back.
Or perhaps it is a person who has never understood why the Gospel is about Jesus saving sinners rather than people proving themselves worthy.
Because none of us outgrows our need for the Gospel.
And if you have been helped by this ministry and want to become part of sustaining and expanding it, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources accessible to people who are hungry for the Word of God.
These resources are meant to nourish faith, strengthen biblical understanding, and encourage spiritual maturity.
And keeping a ministry like this growing requires more than good intentions.
It requires time, work, resources, and the generous support of people who believe that the message of Christ is worth sharing.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, generously, and cheerfully, not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your local church, family responsibilities, and other commitments matter too.
It is the opportunity to participate in work that continually points people back to Jesus.
A book may encourage someone to open Scripture again.
A devotional may reach a believer who has been spiritually exhausted.
An article may help someone recognize a sin they have been hiding.
A Gospel message may become one small part of God's work in drawing a person toward repentance and faith.
We cannot promise how many people will respond.
But we can be faithful in making the truth available.
And that is something worth doing together.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
That is the very truth we are committed to proclaiming.
So give freely if you can.
Share generously if you are moved.
Pray faithfully for this work.
And above all, follow Jesus.
Because one day, every earthly title will lose its importance.
The number of followers we gained will no longer impress us.
The applause we received will grow silent.
The achievements we once considered extraordinary will seem small beside the glory of Christ.
And the question that matters will not be how many people knew our names.
It will be whether we truly belonged to the Savior.
The disciples came back rejoicing that demons knew the authority of Jesus' name.
Jesus redirected their joy to the astonishing privilege of having their own names written in heaven.
Do not miss the difference.
One was a testimony of power exercised through them.
The other was a testimony of grace given to them.
And when you understand that difference, you begin to see why Jesus spoke those unforgettable words.
He was not taking away their joy.
He was leading them to a greater one.
Because the greatest miracle is not that darkness trembles when you speak in Jesus' name. It is that a sinner can be forgiven, redeemed, and welcomed into God's family through Jesus Christ.
And when your final day on earth comes, you will not need the world to remember your name.
You will need the Savior who knows His own.
The world may forget everything you accomplished for Jesus, but nothing in this world is greater than the grace of belonging to Him.
